Approximating the Schr\"odinger equation is vital for analyzing quantum systems, yet it poses significant challenges due to the issue of curse of dimensionality. To address this, researchers have introduced deep learning techniques that use neural networks, with empirical results suggesting that the error converges at the same rate as the standard approximation error, consequently mitigating potential impacts of higher dimensions. This study theoretically validates these findings by examining the generalization error for two-layer neural networks in a specific regression framework relevant to finding Schr\"odinger equation solutions in arbitrary high dimensions. Under specific conditions, new bounds on the generalization error were derived, confirming that the algorithm's total error matches the approximation error rate. These outcomes extend previous works [13, 14] by adopting a broader function class based on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) theory for the theoretical analysis, further supporting the successful application of the deep learning neural network algorithm in solving this problem across various high-dimensional dimensions.

Within each bin, the cosmic-ray direction distribution was fitted to determine the mean direction and standard deviation of the isotropy. This high-energy trend may suggest extragalactic origins for ultra-hight energies.

This paper investigates a model-free reinforcement learning method for adjusting nonlinear optimal regulators for systems subject to additive nonlinear disturbances and measurement noise. To address the absence of a precise mathematical framework and traditional metrics used in classical control design, the proposed strategy is entirely data-driven. It relies on two distinct phases: first, during the "learning" stage, both the original linear and nonlinear control policies are trained using a common reinforcement learning algorithm; secondly, in the second phase, that specific policy is applied to refine the optimal nonlinear control strategy, also via an RL approach. We perform a real-space renormalization group analysis of active nematics, examining both two- and three-dimensional systems to derive the critical exponents for nematic colloids forming nematic clusters. Our findings indicate that dimensionality is a key factor, as the spectral properties of active nematics differ fundamentally between two and three dimensions. In two dimensions, the system exhibits a complex phase behavior: it undergoes an isotropic-nematic transition at a higher concentration threshold before a subsequent nematic-ordered transition is reached at an even higher activity level. Conversely, no ordered phase is stabilized in three dimensions. Furthermore, in the nematic-ordered regime within two dimensions, we identified that the virial exponent generally diverges from its value ($\gamma_{\text{norm}} = 1$) observed in passive nematic systems of the same dimensionality, with specific renormalization group flow analysis allowing for the calculation of the virial exponent's activity-dependent behavior.

While photoevaporation has long been the leading theory for explaining the low-mass driven outflows from young stellar objects (YSOs), recent theoretical studies have explored alternative models based on magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). To distinguish between these competing scenarios, this work aims to propose observations as a critical testing tool. Utilizing MHD simulations of M1.5-class stars like TW Hydrae, maintained at low accretion rates ($10^{-10}$ g/s), we developed two distinct models—one based on photoevaporation and the other on MHD winds. By simulating observations with the proposed Radio Instrument for Planet and Star studies (RIPS) on the upcoming 39-meter Square Kilometre Array Low-frequency Array precursor (SKALP), we assessed TWA's detectability and measured angular resolutions required to resolve both the compact source and the surrounding outflow. For the MHD wind model, MRA imaging would identify a collimated jet extending approximately 3,000 AU. In contrast, wide-field 300 AU long, parabolic-shaped photoevaporative flows would allow astronomers to clearly separate this structure from the central object.

Utilizing a sinusoidal model of speech, this study introduces an unsupervised method for detecting voiced speech and estimating the instantaneous pitch. The proposed technique, which requires no manually tuned parameters and performs reliably across various speech rates and energies, uses a simple Kalman filter to estimate the non-stationary pitch variation and determines voicing thresholds based on one standard deviation of the predicted pitch uncertainty. Empirical evidence suggests this new unsupervised method correlates well with a manually annotated gold standard, yielding similar performance to existing state-of-the-art supervised techniques.

Although convergence cannot be established without minimizing total variation in either parameter, these conditions are typically satisfied in practical scenarios. On convex optimization tasks, our approach mirrors the well-known damped forward–backward algorithm by Parikh and Zhang, allowing it to achieve first-order accuracy. Ultimately, by demonstrating the relationship between this method and a class of inclusion solvers introduced by Cai and others (2020), we prove that the proposed scheme can realize a quantifiable acceleration relative to the standard damped forward–backward method.

Our contribution is novel in analyzing RL decision-making processes that incorporate temporal data, where agents rely on sequences of observations rather than single frames. The proposed framework achieves success in reducing the performance of various pre-trained RL agents that rely on visual inputs.

Distributed machine learning (DML) aims to train a model across multiple devices, making it a critical area with numerous real-world applications and active research. Recent privacy frameworks for geospatial data focus on concealing data collection locations, yet they often fail to safeguard the track itself—the continuous sequence of locations—against attacks that infer subsequent positions from the resulting obscured data. This paper presents the **cpri** (conditional prior privacy) framework, which protects both the collection point and the trajectory between them. By doing so, cpri effectively guards the entire location set and the inter-point information, which prior independent-and-identically-distributed (i.i.d.) approaches could potentially miss.

In medium access control, random protocols utilize statistical multiplexing to handle communication. Moreover, in specific constrained interference environments where the number of potential receivers exceeds those required for transmission plus one, this method degenerates into a pure random access protocol; under these conditions, it delivers the optimal performance with guaranteed constants relative to standard metrics like delay, delay fluctuations, and efficiency in the asymptotic limit of large network scales.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in diverse applications, especially for processing labeled datasets. Yet, obtaining such labels remains both costly and labor-intensive. To address this challenge, pseudo-tagging offers a promising strategy: it utilizes data annotated by humans or experts outside the specific problem domain to label unlabeled samples, thereby facilitating supervised pre-training before transitioning to a final task. An effective method must overcome inherent biases in the initial labeled set during this pre-training phase. However, existing techniques often amplify these dataset-specific characteristics because traditional supervised strategies merely reshuffle training batches, while domain adaptation methods prioritize minimizing discrepancy between pseudo-labeled and newly labeled data, often at the expense of incorporating informative pseudo-labels. To resolve this, our proposed method, called IT-Pseudo, maintains the i.i.d. assumption by sampling a consistent batch size during both the pre-training and final training stages. This ensures a balanced representation of a problem's various aspects appears in every batch, effectively preventing the dominance of initial dataset bias. Additionally, we develop a graph-level bias estimator to guide learning so that pseudo-labels do not overshadow the few true labels. Empirical results across both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that IT-Pseudo excels at leveraging low-cost data across a wide range of semisupervised graph problems, significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods.

Deep learning models for hand-written structured text recognition typically struggle with key and numeric fields, often producing outputs that are plausible but incorrect. This paper introduces a regularization mechanism applied to the recognition pipeline that expends computational budget to reach a given training epoch. We present the initial direct numerical demonstration that confining $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories exhibit the disruption of chiral symmetry alongside confinement. Our analysis examines the prototypical $SO(3)$ gauge theory interacting with fundamental matter fields, which we interpret as bi-fundamental $SO(3) \times SU(N_{c})$ theories by associating them with an $SU(2)$ color factor. We interpret an abrupt transition in $\langle\bar{\psi}\psi\rangle$ as signs of chiral symmetry breaking alongside confinement. Our findings also show that adding an $SU(N_{c})$ factor to the $SO(N_{c})$ gauge group smoothly expands the region of broken chiral symmetry as the strong coupling decreases. These outcomes offer new insights into how non-perturbative effects drive confinement and chiral symmetry breaking across various gauge theories.

Machine learning models are now ubiquitous, frequently supplanting statistical techniques. However, the lack of transparency in these "black box" systems hinders their acceptance in high-stakes domains such as healthcare. To address this, researchers have prioritized developing methods to interpret complex models, specifically for complex decision tree ensembles like Random Forests. While literature exists interpreting individual trees, effective interpretation of entire forests remains an emerging field. Focusing on a key challenge—producing concise, human-understandable explanations for ensemble outputs—this work introduces a solution by adapting Individual Attribution Trees into Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs). Inspired by DACs used in classification, this visualization summarizes a computer's classification confidence across various input features to generate curved graphs. To enable this for regression, we proposed developing an enhancement to the computer algorithm, specifically Disentangled Attribution Curves for Regression (DAC-R), which requires training both individual DACs and an "DAC-Analyzer" to merge them. Evaluating the method with synthetic data and a medical dataset used for healthcare, we measured its accuracy by correlating DAC-R curves against known ground-truth data to correlate with them. The results demonstrate that trained computers can accurately identify and distinguish both complex linear nonlinear relationships and relationships that involve interactions of features.

Federated averaging is a widely adopted framework for distributed machine learning, enabling the aggregation of models trained on distinct data sources. However, due to the inherent opacity of this process, gainers in machine outputs often struggle to verify that no malicious data corrupts the final model, which has spurred the development of verifiable training systems. While such systems exist, they fail to vet the source environments themselves; these solutions allow adversarial parties to inject malicious training data without triggering detection. To address this, we propose Flatee, a new protocol enabling secure, cross-platform federated learning by vetting trusted computation environments. Participating in this system requires each partiser to prove they possess an Intel SGX or AMD SEV trusted execution environment, with the federator receiving a signed attestation of the participant's code. After gathering models, the federator uploads the combined model to a secure remote server within the runner's trusted environment for aggregation. By combining environment verification with the aggregation process, Flatee ensures that good data remains good and bad data is neutralized, effectively preventing attackers from hiding malicious training samples.

This study analyzes the density distribution of low-mass stars in proximity to a central supermassive black hole, specifically within the Milky Way's Galactic Center where Sagittarius A* resides. Tb3Ru3O7 contains alternating spin-3/2 Ru chains and exhibits complex magnetic behavior characterized by spin-canting in the main field, Ising-like chain interactions, single-ion anisotropy, and nonbiased effective random fields. Traditional local functional models in vision are commonly built using Gaussian derivatives; however, their Gaussian foundations restrict their application in periodic tasks, such as edge and texture modeling. Additionally, the periodic nature of these derivatives is usually dampened by derivative orders or smoothing techniques. We introduce a different approach based on modulation theory that represents local functional components as products of periodic functions (either trigonometric or based on hypergeometric functions) and smoothly varying envelope functions. We demonstrate using a neural network framework that this formulation enables efficient generalization across both input space and frequency domains. Furthermore, a derivation using complex differential geometry shows that locally, any functional can be approximated by these products, justifying our method as a geometric universal approximator. This work combines a theoretical framework for modulated periodic functions in the analysis of local properties with a deep learning framework that validates this theory in practical applications.

Deep learning represents a cornerstone artificial intelligence technique that utilizes multi-layer learning machines, such as neural networks, to execute deep functions. When paired with heavy regularization, these models generate "smoothed" decision sheets, leading gradient descent to traverse broader regions of the high-dimensional data. The implications derived from this hypothesis and related geometry hold promise for advancing understanding in machine learning frameworks and may benefit the broader AI community.

Although internet rumors frequently lack empirical supportable predictions, they often embed implicit claims that would be verifiable if they were the focus. This study investigates the high-frequency use of assertions about future events in the face of contradictory evidence within Facebook posts concerning water fluoridation, climate change, and coronavirus vaccines and mortality rates, specifically targeting statements like "proof is being hidden." By applying topic models to analyze correlated future predictions across these posts, the researchers found significant overlaps. This structural similarity suggests a common framework connects these beliefs, which may help explain the entrenched nature of online misinformation.

We propose a novel system for the real-time monitoring of spatio-temporal traffic incidents using geotagged social media posts. Capable of accurately pinpointing incident locations even with sparse data, the system determines extent and duration by analyzing the timing and position of posts, combined with historical traffic patterns to model the incident profile. Incidents are represented specifically via an averaging method that calculates the mean post density along a road segment over a given time interval. To find these road segments with abnormal increases in posted incident information, we employ a specialized profile constructed from a historical pool of geotagged posts, utilizing a non-parametric statistical approach to ensure robust accuracy. Our method's performance and computational efficiency were validated through comparative benchmarking against two other statistical methods and by benchmarking processing speeds.

Future high-precision cosmological observations from the CMB and large-scale structure (LSS) are poised to constrain primary bispectrum shapes with significant confidence. To capitalize on the cross-correlation between these two probes, however, the 800+ realizations currently projected for LSS surveys would require substantial computational resources to process against CMB datasets. To overcome this, we introduce a swift estimator that generates low-count, skewed bispectra by applying machine learning techniques to the full set of CMB non-Gaussian templates. We demonstrate its efficacy using Planck temperature maps and mock large-scale density fields, showing achieved speedsup factors of 100–1000x. The method's capacity to extract the full scientific potential from upcoming projects, such as Euclid, is explored by analyzing one-dimensional observables. In this context, we find that the primary bottleneck for computational efficiency lies not in generating sufficient bispectrum samples, but rather in the need to accurately model the precise alignment and shape of these signals.

This paper presents a Bayesian framework for learning with verifiable adversarial robustness. Within this approach, the posterior distribution over model parameters is refined using evidence derived from the absence of labeled examples that could be perturbed while maintaining accuracy. To make this posterior computable, the authors introduce a Bayesian inference scheme implemented via Markov chain Monte Carlo, which incorporates dynamic certification bounds to handle label distributional shift by adapting to the empirical data. Furthermore, they develop a scalable gradient-based approximation that enables robust training and Bayesian inference on large datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that this method effectively updates priors using real-world dataset characteristics and prior knowledge, successfully establishing a robust bridge between classical Bayesian and deep learning methodologies.

Addressing online rumors in China is particularly challenging given the ubiquitous nature of social media. Various factors contribute to their proliferation, even though specific spread analysis and impact assessment techniques remain underdeveloped. This paper investigates the spread of online rumors regarding the COVID-19 pandemic within Chinese social networks. It employs Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling to discern structural characteristics of the rumor networks, thereby revealing the foundational nature of the spread. Recent research indicates that fast neutrino instability modes, which arise when hydrodynamic effects are negligible, can cause an energy exchange among neutrinos of different types, regions, and helicities within approximately 10^-4 seconds. In deep learning for vision tasks, building network architectures involving convolutional operations and fully connected layers can be explicitly defined using graph theory, where data flows are dictated by these connectivity patterns. Recent developments include designs that concentrate on specific local regions or global features and networks handling recurrent sequences; both are effectively reinterpreted through their respective input-output graph structures. Extending this framework enables the design of networks capable of processing visual data—such as images, video, and the more complex multi-modal visual-text inputs—in the form of dynamic graphs. These graphs possess both data-driven and task-driven properties that undergo significant variation, posing substantial challenges for network engineering, particularly in selecting appropriate aggregation functions along each graph edge. To address this, we introduce a unified and flexible framework termed DGCPN (Dynamic Graph Communication Processing Network), which implements end-to-end learning of both aggregation functions and the underlying graph topology, tailored specifically for multi-modal visual recognition. Evaluated on next-frame prediction, video classification, and visual question answering benchmarks, DGCPN demonstrates superior performance. Furthermore, analyzing the internally learned graph structures offers critical insights into the distinct characteristics and evolution of different visual data representations.

Valued Constraint Optimization Problems (VCOPs) assign specific cost values to every partial assignment for their variables, with the objective of minimizing the total cost for the resulting assignment of all variables. A general-valued optimization problem is defined by an input instance where these local values are drawn from an arbitrary set $\Gamma$; this framework encompasses various specific variants, such as those with cost ratios in $\{0,1\}$ to $10^6$ or $\{0,1,10^6\}$, as well as unnormalized probabilistic constraints. We introduce a technique for the approximate optimization of sparse general-valued problems that guarantees a theoretical performance close to optimal. This method builds on our recent characterization of the structural traits necessary for sparsity to be exploited in specific VCOPs, a property that also enables efficient approximation in these instances. Although the broader application of this exploitation is not yet established for all sparse general-valued problems, we demonstrate that it successfully addresses those satisfying a relatively mild regularity requirement.

Ultimately, TuRanan outperforms prior methods by leveraging simple, energy-efficient voltage reduction that lowers production costs while effectively mitigating side-channel risks. The frequent employment of optical lattices to slow, cool, and trap laser atoms typically relies on a fundamental principle known as the motional Stokes shift, often referred to as the "anti-Sbeck effect." This effect arises because a moving atom encounters and absorbs photons from a moving wavefront within the recoil spread, effectively experiencing a red Doppler shift relative to the laser frequency. Consequently, the atom inhabits a moving lattice structure within its own rest frame that is slower than the physical laser pattern, confining it to regions moving opposite the lab-frame velocity. In this work, we investigate an alternative mechanism for thermal confinement opposed to this classical Doppler cooling through high-resolution time and energy measurements of individual recoil events across full vibrational cycles in optical traps. We observe that atoms trapped by mechanisms other than the anti-Sbeck effect still reach equilibrium at temperatures significantly lower than the natural recoil limit. We propose that this surprising result stems from reduced phase space during the stochastic quantum jumps inherent to repeated photon absorption and emission, suggesting new pathways for ultra-cold trapping methods.

This paper introduces a high-order relationship framework that models direct linkages within cryptocurrency trading networks, specifically between pairs or groups of assets. By examining GLO changes over time in the top 100 cryptocurrencies using an Independent Component Model (ICM), we identify high-order dependencies among clusters of between 2 and 10 coins persisting for hours. Crucially, effective simulation requires identifying these high-order dynamics first; relying solely on pairwise correlations is inadequate. Once high-order effects are accounted for, the residual residual returns exhibit time series characteristics where autocorrelations remain near zero. We observe consistent findings in both bid/ask mid-prices and log-returns. Finally, the study reveals that these high-order connections group together coins sharing similar geographic regions of origin.

This study employs cluster and surface science approaches to analyze ground-state structures and vibrational properties of compact water clusters and their sulfuric acid complexes using density functional theory. While previous studies often relied on the harmonic approximation, this work utilizes finite-difference numerical methods to calculate mass-weighted normal modes, thereby accounting for anharmonicities. Additionally, sampling along these nuclear displacement paths generates probability distributions for atomic positions, allowing us to assess the significance of zero-point fluctuations within these systems. Specific attention is given to how these thermal atomic movements influence the identification of proton transfer events in sulfuric acid models and the magnitude of solvation barriers. Our results indicate that including zero-point fluctuations is critical for accurately predicting solvation features and that the efficacy of solvation depends on both the specific geometry and the relative quantity of water molecules involved.

The thermal Hall reaction, previously ignored in quantum field theory frameworks, emerges from the interaction between particles and thermal fluctuations within static magnetic fields. This work analyzes both particle dynamics and energy transport aspects. We explore parallelisms between heat flux movement and either gravitational pull or central forces, yet such analogies hold only temporarily and require both external forces to be invariant rotationally; however, rotational invariance breaks down due to the presence of the thermal medium itself, thus limiting these gravitational models. Furthermore, the traditional Einstein relation connecting mobility and diffusion coefficients cannot apply to particles undergoing thermal Hall motion, while the relationship remains valid for heat transport. The duration over which Einstein relations approximate correctly diminishes as the thermal Hall angle increases. Additionally, we observe that both particles and heat exhibit memory effects, manifesting as non-Markovian temporal dynamics.

Simplifying complex models is frequently employed as a regularization technique. For instance, in an independent components analysis, we seek to discover linear independent sources that are as "sparse," or minimally non-zero, as possible. Similarly, in manifold learning, we aim to identify a low-dimensional structure to represent the data more efficiently. We explore the question of how to define and reduce computational geometric complexity. We demonstrate that for any norm $p \in [1, \infty)$, there exists a specific "geometric regularizer" that effectively drives models to choose solutions on the extreme boundaries, thereby achieving the minimum possible geometric complexity as defined by this $p$-norm measure of geometric complexity. Consequently, this framework explains why deep learning architectures naturally converge to sparse, sparse solutions (when $p=1$) or edge limit cases (when $p=\infty$), such as why autoencoders become extremely unimodal or variational encodes become deterministic. We further show how to extend this approach to discover directions within subspaces (where $p=1$ yields sparsity) and manifaces (where $p=\infty$ yields manifaces of lower dimensions). Furthermore, we show how to apply these principles to variable selection and clustering.

This paper introduces an innovative degree-degree correlation model for sparse random graphs, specifically targeting the binary deletion channel. Simulation results indicate that our proposed code family matches the best known coders for recovering lost data and possesses a computationally efficient complexity.

We expand the predictive security filter to function effectively at the system level for multiple linear time-invariant (LTI) states and outputs subject to additive Gaussian noise. Unlike traditional predictive filters that require an offline randomized algorithm to determine optimal noise covariance based on a true minimum input, our proposed iterative approach iteratively refines this covariance. This systematic approach guarantees a solution where attack detection at each time step ensures overall attack avoidance across the entire operational timeline. Furthermore, we address scenarios involving both bounded and probabilistic uncertainties within this uncertainty. In experiments using a power system benchmark, we demonstrate the method's capacity to achieve robust security assurance despite a lack of precise knowledge regarding noise levels.

Pretraining data significantly influences a language model's output; yet few studies specifically address its impact on in-context learning. Addressing this gap, we investigate performance variations in in-context learning tasks following the incorporation of different pretraining datasets. Our results indicate that a model's in-context learning ability is not consistently determined by a single dataset but rather varies across tasks and depends on the data composition. Additionally, we observe that a diverse range of abilities is supported in a combined corpus containing in-context learning data, encyclopedic content, and domain-specific materials, yet distinct correlations emerge between corpus types and specific performance outcomes. At its core, the success of a model depends on securing a strong understanding of the underlying structure and its associated distribution through the chosen corpus. Based on these observations, we propose strategies to enhance both efficiency and performance in in-context learning across various tasks.

This study introduces a method for generating synthetic speech using a zero-shot approach with a new kind of encoder based on transcripts from perceptual acoustic units. Additionally, we generate 1.25 million speaker-independent samples, doubling the available speaker-independent data for research.

This study addresses a dynamic system optimization problem featuring system dynamics, state and control constraints, and both finite and continuous time. Our primary goal is to develop an efficient method for solving this optimization task. We begin by constructing a data-driven model of the system dynamics utilizing a relaxation based on McCormen Envelopes and applying a computational complexity- and gain-limit-based selection strategy to choose appropriate grid points for these envelopes. Building on this data-driven approximation, we design an iterative multi-stage optimization scheme that guarantees a convergent sequence of feasible solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that each individual stage can be resolved in real-time and provide a theoretical upper bound for the number of optimization stages required to converge.

Recent research by Gulyaev demonstrated that the Duflovo-Siskind (DFS) framework can expand a quantum system's state space without altering its logical operations under a specific unitary group. Using this system in an probabilistic context, Gulyaev showed that state spaces can be strictly constrained: two quantum states can be transformed into one another via a CNOT gate only if they remain identical when the target is in state $|0\rangle$, due to the impossibility of decomposing the CNOT into fully executable processes while this condition isn't met, a concept referred to as probabilical causality. This paper explores such principles, applying the Gulyaev system and similar constructs like the Su-Kim system, which also enable the down-conversion of a single photon into two. These probabilical causality restrictions offer both theoretical insights and practical utility: they clarify constraints within quantum theory and limit the achievable precision of quantum states through characterizations of high fidelity to desired targets via probabilical causality.

Decentralized optimization has seen significant development in recent years; however, Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) remains vulnerable to perturbations caused by data noise or distributional shifts, which can degrade optimization performance. To address this vulnerability, we introduce DR-DSGD, a novel robust training algorithm designed for environments affected by uncertainty. DR-DrDSG combines two key strategies: a regularized aggregation method applied at communication steps and the Wasserstein metric used to construct robust aggregation sets. By analyzing this algorithm, we determine its convergence rate and provide a computational complexity analysis. Furthermore, we validate DR-DSGD through experiments on synthetic data and real-world applications, including support vector machines and deep neural networks, utilizing diverse datasets and topological structures to demonstrate its robustness.

In scientific machine learning (SML), researchers aim to emulate or extend physical laws by inferring them from data. A critical area of focus involves quantifying prediction uncertainty—encompassing both aleatoric (irreducible) uncertainty arising from inherent data randomness and epistemic (reducible) uncertainty stemming from limitations in data or model capacity. By utilizing a dedicated benchmark based on a classic ordinary differential equation (ODE) case study, we conduct wide-ranging comparisons of different uncertainty quantification methodologies. The widespread popularity of machine learning has led to extensive data collection within mobile environments. Federated Learning (FL) offers a robust method for training global models directly on this dispersed data while ensuring strict user privacy. However, FL remains vulnerable to attacks originating from malicious clients, which can degrade both model accuracy and user security. Furthermore, FL systems are often susceptible to bias; for instance, if only wealthy users possess the resources to upgrade their devices and software, the resulting global model may underperform on the data of poorer populations, a known issue of "data heterogeneity."

Addressing these challenges, this paper introduces FLVoogd, a novel system that simultaneously counters FL bias and protects user anonymity. FLVoogd adapts the classic Voigt estimator by modifying the aggregation process to utilize encrypted differences between local models rather than raw models. The system ensures secure communication between devices and the central server, simultaneously guaranteeing both communication and location privacy for the users. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that FLVoogd outperforms existing methods, achieving superior convergence rates and maintaining resilience even when targeted by biased attack scenarios.

Object-oriented programming remains the dominant paradigm widely adopted by developers. DynaSOAr achieves superior allocation efficiency by utilizing a multi-level allocation scheme that partitions the global memory into multiple frames, where each frame holds class-specific free pointer arrays. Stagnant (frozen disordered) scalar fields on a sphere are commonly employed as model frameworks for various natural phenomena, including the magnetic and gravitational potentials of celestial bodies as well as subsurface oil reservoirs. Acquiring measurements of these fields is typically done via staggered sensor arrays; however, due to high costs, the achieved resolution is often sparse and low to the ground. Utilizing these stagnant fields as regression targets, this research investigates several machine learning EDA algorithms, specifically examining their capacity for generalizing across different sphere geometries and their efficiency in reducing field estimation errors. While many algorithms are introduced, we identify the most viable candidate: one-step recurrent neural networks, dubbed the "Sphere Recurrent Unit" (SRU). This model leverages group-theoretic group theory within the rotation group $SO(3)$ to enforce equivariance under rotations, thereby navigating the complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces inherent in deep learning more effectively. Numerical results indicate that the SRU significantly outperforms numerous baseline approaches in sphere regression tasks, making it a powerful and practical instrument for interpolating random stagnant datasets on the sphere while taking advantage of inherent group symmetries.

Neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases involve the accumulation of misfolded proteins in neurons, thereby disrupting normal cellular function. For specific proteins like amyloid-beta, efficient transport between them is essential; however, for others, such as tau, this transport is hindered. A key objective in research is to identify the genetic and environmental factors that influence this neuronal transportation mechanism. In this study, a novel mathematical framework for a diffusive-protein system is developed to simulate healthy neuronal states and isolate environmental and genetic variables capable of regulating protein transport and preventing the formation transport jams—aggregates caused by proteins overwhelming their proteins carriers. Within each cell, a set of partial differential equations (PDEs) is employed to model the interaction and flow of proteins. These physics-based constraints are integrated into an optimization model designed to determine the most effective genetic or environmental modifications capable of regulating protein transport and mitigating pathological jams. Finally, a solution algorithm addressing these nonlinear, PDE-constrained optimization challenges is designed and tested on a synthetic neuron, with results demonstrating that the proposed mathematical approach effectively regulates protein transport and prevents neuronal jams.

Although Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become dominant for processing graph data, the design principle underlying graph convolution remains elusive. Existing literature typically defines a graph convolution as an operation that computes node features using local graph structures and input signals, yet this approach conflicts with both spatial and frequency perspectives, presenting conceptual challenges that impede comprehensive understanding. This work aims to clarify the graphical convolution process from an intuitive filter-matching methodology. Furthermore, it provides a detailed analysis of graph convolution within the frequency domain, examining how spectral characteristics of graph shift operators dictate filtering properties and graph convolution properties. Additionally, it explores various graph polynomial filters demonstrates their superior efficacy in capturing intricate, complex patterns in data. Ultimately, it establishes a clear connection between polynomial-based operations and GCNs, revealing the former's advantage in comprehending the fundamental mechanics behind the latter.

Natural language processing represents a field with broad potential applications that relies heavily on accurate language parsing. Despite significant recent strides in neural parsing models, these advancements are hindered by dependencies on external resources—such as context-free grammars, dependency schemas, or rule-based information—alongside substantial high-compute training costs. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a self-contained self-learning approach for neural parsing that eliminates all external dependencies. Unlike prior self-supervised methods confined to a unsupervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning paradigm, our self-trained method employs a specialized supervised self-training algorithm. This scheme iteratively expands training sets by generating parsed structures from a model which is subsequently refined. To facilitate this supervised self-training, we developed a tailored self-trainer that employs a universal self-consistent check.
